chapter_theme: Under the heading மறை பிறர் அறியாமை, six verses on keeping secrets: kinship and friendship are no ground for disclosure, a mean confidant chosen over worthy kin is a drum struck, love must be known before one confides, everyone passes on what he hears, only the noble keep a secret, and even the affectionate must be examined first.

177.reading: The wise do not, going on the ground that someone is kin or friend, trust him with their weak point, for even the lord who rides the victorious bird and strode across the world did what served his ends.
177.nuance: அற்றம் is the exposed or unguarded point, the thing one must hide; the verse refuses kinship and friendship as grounds for disclosing it. The proof is drawn from a god: if even he acted for his own advantage, no lesser bond is a guarantee. The sense of சீர்ந்தது is not certain; 'what suited him' is a reading from context.

pazhamozhi.literal: there is no one who does not do what suits him

story.act: the lord who rides the victorious bird and strode over the world, who even so did what served his purpose
story.tradition: by tradition Vishnu, the Garuda-rider, whose striding of the worlds is the Vamana episode in which he won the earth from Mahabali by a request; the verse names neither

pazhamozhi.applied_to: since everyone, even a god, acts for advantage, kinship or friendship is no ground for revealing one's weak point

178.reading: When one's own people, rich in every excellence, are at hand, to pick out a man with no excellence of mind, take him aside into one's secret counsel and not put him away is like setting the drumstick to the drum's face.
178.nuance: The fault lies with the one who chose the confidant: passing over worthy kin for a small-minded outsider is itself the beating of the drum, so the leak is the chooser's own act. The syntax of மாற்றா தொழிதல் (not removing him) is loose.

pazhamozhi.literal: it is the way of putting the stick to the drum's face

story.act: no story; the proverb is the act of readying a drum to be sounded

pazhamozhi.applied_to: confiding a secret to a man of mean mind is preparing its public announcement

179.reading: One should not run ahead to tell one's secret to anyone at all before knowing their love, for no one follows the track of an antelope to carry it off safe, only to kill it as the man who means to eat it kills.
179.nuance: The image makes the over-eager listener a hunter on the trail: the one who pursues another's secret pursues it to use it. The construction of lines 2-4 (தின்குறுவான் கொல்வாங்குக் கொன்றபின் அல்லது) is compressed and the reading of the image is tentative.

pazhamozhi.literal: no one follows an antelope's path to take it away alive

story.act: no story; the hunter tracks the antelope only to kill and eat it

pazhamozhi.applied_to: one who has not shown love and seeks a secret seeks it to do harm, so it is not to be told before love is known

180.reading: Addressing a woman with cloud-like hair and golden bangles, the verse says that even among those who keep friendship pleasantly there is no one who does not pass on what he has heard, and so the worthy do not tell their secret to the base.
180.nuance: The first half claims more than the proverb: it is not only the base but anyone, even a pleasant friend, who carries on what he hears. The proverb then narrows the rule to the base, so the verse moves from a general distrust to a practical line drawn at the mean. உயவாது shares the root of the Kural's உய்த்து (carrying a secret on).

pazhamozhi.literal: they do not tell a secret to the base

story.act: no story; the proverb states the practice of the worthy (சான்றோர்)

pazhamozhi.applied_to: since what is heard is always passed on, the worthy keep their secrets from the base

181.reading: Addressing the lord of the great mountain land, the verse says that only the noble keep the precious secret that others must not know, and that telling it to the small of heart is like setting cotton on top of a palmyra and carding it loose.
181.nuance: Cotton fluffed on a palm-top is scattered by the wind beyond any gathering back; the image stresses that the loss cannot be undone and spreads in every direction. Keeping a secret is named as a mark of the ஆன்றோர், not merely a prudence.

pazhamozhi.literal: it is like placing cotton on a palmyra and carding it

story.act: no story; cotton carded at a height is blown abroad

pazhamozhi.applied_to: a secret told to the small-hearted is scattered past recovery

182.reading: There is no need to speak one's confidences to the hostile who stand apart as strangers, like the dead, and even with the affectionate, one who trusts without examining perishes.
182.nuance: The verse moves from the obvious case, the estranged, to the hard one, the loving, and makes examination necessary even there. தஞ்சம் here is what one leans on, the matter one confides; முளிந்தார் (the withered, dried up) is a rare figure for those whose regard has died.

pazhamozhi.literal: one who trusts without having examined will perish

story.act: no story; the proverb states the fate of trust without testing

pazhamozhi.applied_to: even those who show affection must be examined before one confides in them

links.note: Kural 506 warns against trusting those cut off from kin, since ties make a person accountable; Pazhamozhi 177 says kinship or friendship is no ground for trusting anyone with one's weak point.
links.teaches: Together they show ties as a necessary but not sufficient condition of trust: the kinless are not to be trusted, yet kin are not to be trusted with one's exposed point either, since even a god acted for his own ends.
links.list_adds: its proverb grounds the limit in a universal claim proved from a god's conduct, so the couplet's reliance on attachment meets a rule that self-interest outruns every bond.

links.note: Kural 1076 likens the base to a beaten drum that proclaims every secret heard; Pazhamozhi 178 likens the choosing of a mean confidant to putting the stick to the drum.
links.teaches: The drum image moves from the base man to his chooser: the Kural blames the drum for sounding, Pazhamozhi blames the one who sets the stick to it, so the leak begins in a bad choice of confidant over worthy kin.
links.list_adds: it sets the mean confidant against kin rich in excellence, turning the couplet's description of the base into a fault of selection by the one who confides.

links.note: Kural 1076 makes carrying on (உய்த்து) secrets the mark of the base; Pazhamozhi 180 says that even pleasant friends cannot refrain from passing on (உயவாது) what they heard, then restricts the rule to the base.
links.teaches: Read with the Kural, the verse shows the trait the couplet confines to the base is near-universal, so keeping secrets from the base is a minimum measure, not a sufficient safeguard.
links.list_adds: it widens the couplet's claim from the base to everyone, even agreeable friends, before narrowing it again in the proverb, a turn the couplet lacks.

links.note: Thirikadugam 55 counts a friendship that does not keep a weighty secret as a spy; Pazhamozhi 180 says that even among pleasant friends no one keeps back what he heard.
links.teaches: Together they show that the leaking friend is not a rare traitor but the common case, which is why a counted work can number him among the spies inside one's circle.

links.note: Kural 847 says the man without understanding who lets slip the precious secret (அருமறை) harms himself; Pazhamozhi 181 says telling the precious secret (அருமறை) to the small-hearted is cotton carded on a palm-top.
links.teaches: The pair names one concrete way the secret slips: handing it to a small heart, and the image shows why the harm the Kural calls self-inflicted cannot be recalled once done.
links.list_adds: it opposes the noble keepers to the small-hearted hearers, adding to the couplet's lone fool a ranking of who can hold a secret at all.

links.note: Kural 509 bids one trust no one without examination; Pazhamozhi 182 applies this even to the affectionate and says the unexamined truster perishes.
links.teaches: The pairing extends the Kural's rule to the case where it is hardest to keep, affection, and fixes the stake at death rather than mere trouble.
links.list_adds: it ranks the hostile, who need no testing because they are plainly not to be told, below the affectionate, who must be tested, a contrast the couplet does not draw.

links.note: Pazhamozhi 179 permits telling a secret once the hearer's love is known; Naladiyar 127 asks who has the power to know another's mind, since mind and deed differ.
links.teaches: Held together they show the condition Pazhamozhi sets may never be met: if love cannot be read from conduct, the counsel to wait for known love becomes a counsel of near-total silence.
links.list_adds: the Naladiyar quatrain denies the knowledge of minds that Pazhamozhi's proverb of the hunting trail presupposes can be had.

new_concepts.gloss: the secret or confidence to be kept from others; its guarding and its disclosure
new_concepts.label_source: the verses use the word (Pazhamozhi 178-181) and the heading மறை பிறர் அறியாமை

source_issues: 177 line 4: சீர்ந்தது is a rare form; its sense (what suits or profits one) is inferred from context.
179 lines 3-4: the quotation opens at உயக்கொண்டு, leaving the hunter clause (தின்குறுவான் கொல்வாங்குக் கொன்றபின் அல்லது) outside though it belongs to the image; the syntax is compressed.
180 line 4: the quotation opens after சான்றோர், which is the subject of the proverb's verb உரையார்.
